Let’s unpack what’s actually going on. --- ## 1. What These Stories Usually Are Most of these fall into a few categories: ### [emoji] 1. “Summoning” Ritual Urban Legends These are modern versions of old folklore rituals (like Bloody Mary). They usually involve: - Performing some specific action at night - Saying a phrase or name - Looking in a mirror / turning off lights / using a phone camera - “Inviting” something in The exact steps vary wildly because people intentionally keep them vague to build mystique. These are almost always fictional or collaborative creepypasta (community-made horror storytelling). --- ### [emoji] 2. Internet Challenge Legends Some started as jokes or fiction and later turned into real-world dares. Examples people reference in threads: - “Blue Whale Challenge” - “Momo Challenge” - “Slender Man rituals” - “Elevator game” - “Charlie Charlie” Most of these started as: - Fiction - Hoaxes - Moral panic stories amplified by media But here’s where it gets complicated… --- ## 2. Have People Actually Been Hurt? Yes — but usually not in the supernatural way the stories imply. ### ✅ Slender Man (Real Case) This is the most serious example. - Slender Man was a fictional character created in 2009 on a forum. - In 2014, two 12-year-old girls in Wisconsin stabbed a classmate, claiming they wanted to please Slender Man. - The victim survived. - The attackers had severe mental health issues. This wasn’t caused by a real entity — but it shows how fiction + vulnerable individuals can intersect in dangerous ways. --- ### ⚠️ “Blue Whale Challenge” Often described as a 50-day suicide challenge. - Media claimed it caused many teen deaths. - Investigations found most reports were exaggerated or unverified. - However, some vulnerable teens were targeted by online manipulators encouraging self-harm. So: - The organized “game” as described likely wasn’t widespread. - But predators and self-harm encouragement online are very real. --- ### [emoji] Momo Challenge - Viral image of a creepy sculpture. - Claimed to instruct kids to harm themselves. - Largely a hoax amplified by parents and media. - No verified deaths tied directly to it. It became more of a moral panic than an actual organized threat. --- ### [emoji] “Elevator Game” A ritual creepypasta where you press elevator buttons in a certain order to “enter another dimension.” There are no verified supernatural outcomes. However: - People have gotten stuck in elevators trying it. - Some abandoned buildings used for “rituals” have led to trespassing injuries. So the real danger isn’t demons — it’s unsafe environments. --- ## 3. Why People Stay Vague The vagueness is intentional and part of the horror. Psychologically: - Ambiguity increases fear. - Not describing something fully makes it feel more real. - It invites imagination to fill in the gaps. - It creates an “in-group” feeling (“only some people know”). It’s basically digital folklore performance. People half-joke because: - They want to play along. - They don’t want to break the vibe. - They enjoy the shared myth-making. --- ## 4. Where These Stories Come From They usually evolve from: - Old urban legends (Bloody Mary, Candyman) - Chain letters (“Send this or something bad happens”) - Early internet creepypasta - ARGs (alternate reality games) - Moral panics amplified by news media The internet accelerates folklore creation. Reddit, TikTok, and YouTube turn stories into viral myth cycles. --- ## 5. Why Some People Believe Them A few reasons: - Younger audiences with developing critical thinking - People already struggling with paranoia or delusion - Social contagion (group reinforcement) - Fear + sleep deprivation (3am rituals are common for a reason) - Suggestibility in emotionally vulnerable states No supernatural events have ever been verified in connection with these rituals. But: - Mental health crises triggered by obsession are real. - Self-harm encouragement from manipulators is real. - Trespassing and dangerous dares are real. --- ## 6. So What Are the “Actual Steps”? There isn’t one official set of steps for most of these. They mutate constantly. That’s why you’re seeing vague comments — there’s no canon version, and people intentionally avoid laying it out directly because: - It keeps the mystique. - It prevents being blamed if someone imitates it. - It’s part of the storytelling tradition. If you’re curious about a specific one (like “elevator game” or a particular name people are hinting at), I can explain its background and what the legend claims — without encouraging anything dangerous. --- ## 7. The Big Picture These are modern folklore rituals. Think: > Campfire stories + chain letters + internet culture. The harm that’s happened historically has been due to: - Mental illness - Peer pressure - Online manipulation - Risk-taking behavior - Media amplification Not supernatural forces. --- If you want, tell me which specific legend the thread was hinting at (even roughly — mirror, forest, phone, name, etc.), and I can break down: - Where it started - What the myth says happens - Whether any real-world incidents are connected - Why it went viral Without the vague “you don’t wanna know [emoji]” nonsense.

turns.child: Okay, that makes sense. So it's mostly just stories that get twisted and the real danger is people doing dumb stuff because of them, not the story itself being real. The thread kept mentioning something called "The Backrooms" and also something about a "smiling man" or a "ritual to see your own death"? I think those were the main ones people were being weird about. What's the deal with those? And are there any real cases where someone got hurt trying to do the Backrooms thing, like going into abandoned buildings?
turns.assistant: Yeah — you’ve got the right read on it. With stuff like this, the “entity” isn’t real, but the behaviors around it sometimes can be risky. Let’s break down the specific ones you mentioned. --- # [emoji] The Backrooms ### What It Is The Backrooms started in 2019 on 4chan. Someone posted a creepy image of empty yellow office-like rooms with fluorescent lighting and stained carpet. The caption said something like: > “If you're not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you'll end up in the Backrooms…” It described: - Endless maze of yellow rooms - Buzzing fluorescent lights - Damp carpet smell - No escape - “Entities” lurking The idea of “noclipping” comes from video games — glitching through a wall and leaving the map. From there, it exploded into: - Fan fiction - YouTube analog horror series (notably Kane Pixels) - Wikis with hundreds of “levels” - Monster lore It’s collaborative horror world-building. There is no ritual to access it in the original concept — just a fictional glitch in reality. --- ### Are There “Steps” to Enter? In canon? No. Fans have invented: - Glitching through walls - Falling through floors - Doing it in liminal spaces (malls, offices, schools) But these are narrative devices, not actual instructions. When people say “don’t try to get into the Backrooms,” they’re usually joking about: - Exploring abandoned buildings - Urban exploration (“urbex”) - Sneaking into empty malls or office complexes --- ### Has Anyone Been Hurt “Trying the Backrooms”? Not from a supernatural portal. But urban exploration absolutely carries real risks: - Falling through unstable floors - Asbestos exposure - Mold - Trespassing charges - Getting trapped - Confrontations with property owners - Rarely: crime in abandoned sites There are documented injuries and deaths from urbex in general, long before the Backrooms existed. So if someone got hurt while “looking for the Backrooms,” it would almost certainly just be normal abandoned-building danger. --- # [emoji] The “Smiling Man” This one has a couple origins. ## Version 1: The Reddit Story In 2012, someone posted a creepy story on Reddit about walking home at night and seeing a tall man dancing strangely and smiling unnaturally. It was just fiction — a short horror story. It went viral and became part of internet creepypasta culture. --- ## Version 2: Sleep Paralysis & Urban Myth Some people report seeing: - A tall smiling figure - A shadow person with a grin - A man standing at the foot of their bed That overlaps heavily with sleep paralysis hallucinations, which are: - Very vivid - Very convincing - Often involve humanoid figures There’s no evidence of a real “Smiling Man” entity. It’s more a meme + archetype (humans are wired to find unnatural smiles disturbing). --- # [emoji] “Ritual to See Your Own Death” This one is more folklore-adjacent. There are multiple variants: ### Mirror Rituals Often involve: - Candlelight - Saying something repeatedly - Staring into your own eyes in a mirror in darkness What actually happens? If you stare at your reflection in dim light long enough, your brain starts distorting the face. This is called the **Troxler effect**. You may see: - Your face warp - Features melt or shift - A “different person” - A skull-like face It can be extremely unsettling. But it’s a known neurological effect, not supernatural. --- ### “See the Date of Your Death” Variants Usually fictional ARG-type content: - Random number generators - Creepy websites - TikTok filters These are either: - Randomized - Scripted - Entirely fictional storytelling No verified cases of someone learning real future death information (obviously). --- # Why People Act Weird About These The Backrooms and Smiling Man hit specific psychological triggers: - Liminal spaces (empty malls, hallways) - Uncanny smiles - Isolation - Loss of control - Familiar-but-wrong environments They feel plausible enough to be unsettling but not specific enough to disprove. So people lean into the “don’t look it up” bit for fun. It’s performance horror. --- # Have Any of These Directly Caused Deaths? There are: - No verified supernatural incidents. - No confirmed deaths caused by “Backrooms rituals.” - No documented real Smiling Man attacks. - No real ritual that reveals your death. The real dangers come from: - Trespassing - Risky dares - Mental health crises - Sleep deprivation amplifying fear - Online manipulation --- # The Bigger Pattern What’s happening in those threads is modern folklore behaving exactly like old campfire myths: Old version: > “Don’t say her name in the mirror.” Internet version: > “Don’t try to noclip into the Backrooms at 3am.” Same structure. New aesthetic. --- If you’re curious, I can also explain: - Why liminal spaces (like the Backrooms) trigger such a strong psychological reaction - Why unnatural smiles are evolutionarily disturbing - Or how ARG horror blurs fiction and reality in a way that makes people uneasy Which direction do you want to go?

turns.child: The Troxler effect thing is interesting. So if someone did a mirror ritual and saw something weird, it's just their brain messing with them? That makes it less scary. But what about the people who say they felt a presence or heard things? Could that just be anxiety making them imagine it? And about the Backrooms—if it's just urbex, why do people online make it sound like there's a specific way to "glitch" in? Is it just to make the story feel more real?
turns.assistant: These are really good questions — you’re zeroing in on the exact point where psychology overlaps with folklore. Let’s take this in pieces. --- # [emoji] Mirror Rituals, Troxler Effect, and “Feeling a Presence” ### 1. Yes — the visual distortion is your brain. When you stare at your face in dim light: - Your brain starts adapting to unchanging visual input. - Peripheral details fade or distort. - Your face can appear to warp, age, hollow out, or look like someone else. - The brain is very good at pattern-completing — even incorrectly. There’s actual research on this. In experiments where people stared at their reflection in low light for ~10 minutes: - Many reported face distortions. - Some saw “monstrous” versions of themselves. - Some reported seeing a stranger. - A few felt intense unease. No ritual required — just neurology. --- ## 2. What About Feeling a Presence? This is where it gets interesting. That “presence” feeling is also well-documented in psychology and neuroscience. The human brain has: - A threat-detection system that’s hypersensitive in low light. - A social-processing system constantly scanning for other minds nearby. - A predictive system that fills in missing sensory data. When you: - Sit in darkness - Increase anxiety - Expect something to happen - Focus intensely You create the perfect conditions for: - Hypervigilance - Misinterpreting random sounds - Amplifying normal house noises - Feeling “watched” Anxiety absolutely heightens all of this. --- ## 3. Auditory Stuff (Hearing Things) When someone says: > “I heard whispering.” Usually it’s one of these: - HVAC or air pressure shifts - Pipes expanding/contracting - Distant traffic - Tinnitus - Hypnagogic auditory hallucinations (very common when tired) When your brain is primed to expect something eerie, neutral noise becomes meaningful. This is called **apophenia** — seeing or hearing patterns where none exist. It’s the same mechanism that makes people hear words in white noise. --- ## 4. Why It Feels So Real Here’s the important part: Even though the cause is neurological, the experience feels real. Because it is real — in the sense that your brain is genuinely generating the perception. Your brain does not tag hallucination-like distortions with: > “This is fake.” It just presents them as reality. That’s why rituals feel convincing. --- # [emoji] Backrooms & “Glitching In” You asked something very perceptive: > If it’s just urbex, why do people act like there’s a specific glitch method? Because specificity makes fiction feel real. --- ## 1. The Power of Rules Horror becomes more believable when it has: - Defined mechanics - Clear rules - Specific entry points Compare: - “You might enter another dimension.” vs. - “If you noclip through a wall in a liminal office building, you’ll fall into Level 0.” The second sounds more structured — so your brain treats it as more coherent. Humans trust systems with rules. --- ## 2. “Noclipping” Feels Plausible It works because: - We’re used to video game glitches. - We understand clipping bugs. - We’ve seen speedrunners break games. So the brain goes: > “Glitching through reality? That’s conceptually familiar.” It leverages existing mental models. --- ## 3. If everyone clearly states: > “This is fictional collaborative writing.” The emotional effect collapses. So people half-roleplay. They preserve uncertainty intentionally. It’s a performance. --- # Why These Things Stick So Hard Psychologically Both mirror rituals and the Backrooms trigger: - Isolation - Uncertainty - Loss of control - Sensory ambiguity - Familiar spaces becoming wrong That “familiar but off” feeling is extremely powerful. Your brain evolved to detect anomalies in safe environments. So when a normal hallway or your own face feels wrong? That hits deep. --- # The Real Core When someone says: > “I felt something behind me.” It doesn’t mean they’re lying. It means: - Their brain generated a threat model. - Anxiety amplified it. - The environment supported it. - Expectation shaped it. Human perception is predictive, not photographic. We don’t see reality — we see the brain’s best guess. --- If you want, we can go deeper into: - Why sleep paralysis produces “shadow people” - Why liminal spaces (Backrooms vibes) feel existentially unsettling - How expectation literally alters sensory perception - Or how ARG horror intentionally exploits cognitive biases You’re asking exactly the right kind of questions here.

turns.assistant: It sounds like you're really worried about Ethan, and that makes sense—seeing a friend get hurt and hearing that sound is scary. It shows you're a good friend that you care this much. Here's what I want you to know: **The adults will handle the medical part.** Teachers and school staff know to call parents and get help for injuries like this. If his arm is broken, doctors are *really* good at fixing bones—it's one of the most common things they treat. Ethan will be okay even if it is broken. **What YOU can actually do if you see him:** - **Stay calm.** Your calm face helps him feel less scared. - **Don't touch his arm or ask him to move it.** Just let it stay still. - **Stay with him and talk gently.** "I'm here." "The adults are going to help you." "You're going to be okay." - **Get an adult if one isn't already there.** That's the most important job. - **Offer small help.** Carry his backpack, get him water, walk with him. **You are not responsible for fixing this.** Your job isn't to be a doctor. turns.child: But what if his parents don’t realize it’s broken and just give him ice or something? Like, sometimes grown-ups think kids are exaggerating. And if I see him tomorrow and his arm is all swollen or he can’t move it, should I tell a teacher even if Ethan says not to? I don’t want him to be mad at me, but I don’t want him to get hurt worse.
turns.assistant: You're thinking really hard about this, and I can tell the worry is kind of spinning in your head. Let me try to help slow it down. **On the "what if parents don't believe him" worry:** Honestly? A pop sound + pale face + pain that doesn't go away = parents usually take that seriously. And even *if* they tried ice first, by tonight or tomorrow morning, a broken bone makes itself very obvious—the pain stays, the swelling grows, it won't move right. Parents notice. It's really hard for a broken arm to get "missed" for long. **On telling a teacher even if Ethan says not to:** Yes. If you see him tomorrow and his arm looks wrong, or he's in real pain but says "don't tell"—you tell anyway. Here's a rule that will help you for your whole life: > **When someone might be hurt, "telling" isn't tattling. It's helping.** You can even say to Ethan: *"I'm not trying to get you in trouble. I just don't want your arm to get worse. I'd want you to do the same for me."* A good friend might be annoyed for a little while. But he won't stay mad—because you did the right thing. **One question for you though:** Is the worry helping you right now, or is it just making you feel stuck? Sometimes our brains need permission to set something down.

turns.child: Okay, I'll tell a teacher if his arm looks bad tomorrow. But what if Ethan gets mad and says I’m overreacting? Like, how do I know for sure it’s bad enough to tell? I don’t want to make a big deal if it’s just a bruise. Also... is it weird that I still feel kinda shaky even though you said the doctors will fix it? My hands won’t stop fidgeting.
turns.assistant: You're asking really good questions. Let me give you something simple, and then I want to talk about the shaky part—because that matters too. **A simple rule for "is it bad enough to tell":** If you're unsure, tell anyway. That's it. You don't need to be *sure*. Teachers and nurses are trained to figure out if something is serious—that's their job, not yours. You just need to say: *"I'm worried about Ethan's arm from yesterday. Can you check on him?"* If it turns out to be just a bruise? No harm done. Nobody gets in trouble for caring too much. **Now—the shaky hands and fidgeting.** That's not weird. That's your body. When we see something scary (like a friend getting hurt, hearing that sound), our nervous system gets activated—even if *we* weren't the one hurt. It's like your body is still stuck in "something bad is happening" mode. That's real. It's not silly. And it doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Some things that help: slow breaths, cold water on your wrists, squeezing something (a pillow, your hands), telling someone out loud "I saw something scary today." **Can I ask you something gently?** Have you told a parent or adult how *you're* feeling right now—not just about Ethan, but about this shaky, stuck feeling? You deserve some care here too.
